## Accessibility Audit Cost

Accessible.org web accessibility audits cost $100 – $250 per page (or screen) and $25 – $100 for light pages/screens. Our audits follow best practices for ADA and EAA compliance. Our audit price is based on comprehensive manual evaluation using the WCAG 2.1 AA standard (or WCAG 2.2 AA). Audits are conducted in desktop environment with the client option to add mobile.

Our website accessibility audits are fully manual, formal evaluations conducted by technical accessibility experts who evaluate your website or other digital assets against WCAG 2.0 AA, WCAG 2.1 AA, or WCAG 2.2 AA standards.

Scope typically does not include all pages or screens, but rather a representative sample.

We use an automated scan as a review to ensure all issues correctly identified by a scan are included in our final audit report.

All Accessible.org auditors are certified DHS Trusted Testers. The DHS Trusted Tester Process is a manual test approach that aligns with the ICT Testing Baseline, and provides repeatable and reliable conformance test results.

### Digital Assets Audited

Accessible.org can audit all types of digital assets:

- Websites

- Web pages

- Web apps

- Mobile apps

- Platforms

- Dashboards

- Software

- Games

- Widgets

- Elements

- Components

- Portals

Accessible.org uses the following methodologies and environments when evaluating your digital asset(s):

- Screen Reader Testing

- Keyboard Testing

- Visual Inspection

- Code Inspection

- Automated Scan:

- AXE

- Color Contrast Analyzer Tool

- Browser Zoom:

- 200%

- 400%

- Browser Environments:

## What Your Accessibility Audit Price Covers

- ### $500 Quick Audit

 Up to 5 page templates, automated and manual spot checks, and a top-10 issues report mapped to WCAG 2.2. Best for small sites that need a first baseline.

- ### $2,000 Complete Audit

 Up to 25 templates or key user flows, full manual testing in JAWS, NVDA and VoiceOver, a re-test of fixed issues and an accessibility statement draft.

- ### Fixed Price, Agreed In Writing

 No hourly billing. The price is agreed before work starts, and the same packages cover WCAG 2.2, ADA, Section 508 and EN 301 549.

- ### Not Sure Yet? Talk First

 The free 30-minute call is for scoping and a quote. The $100 hour is a technical session: an audit walkthrough, time with your developer or a live site review.

 Cost Factors

## What Changes the Cost of an Accessibility Audit

- ### Templates and user flows, not URL count

 A large blog built on a handful of templates can cost less to audit than a small web app with sign-up, search, checkout and a dashboard.

- ### Interactive components

 Carts, filters, modals, date pickers, chat widgets and third-party embeds need keyboard and screen reader testing. Most blockers hide here, so the Complete Audit covers them with JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver and keyboard-only passes.

- ### The standard you have to meet

 ADA Title II points to WCAG 2.1 AA, Section 508 to WCAG 2.0 AA and the EAA to EN 301 549. The same packages cover every standard.

- ### Documents and PDFs

 PDFs, Word and PowerPoint files are tested separately from web pages, including NVDA screen reader passes. PDF remediation is quoted after scoping.

- ### Procurement paperwork

 A VPAT or Accessibility Conformance Report is quoted on top of the audit, because every criterion has to be documented.

- ### Fixes and re-tests

 Fixing issues is a separate, quoted piece of work, done by your team or ours. The Complete Audit includes a re-test of fixed issues so you leave with evidence.

 Worth The Cost?

## Accessibility Audit vs Lawsuit Costs and Free Scans

### Is an Accessibility Audit Cheaper Than an ADA Lawsuit?

Lawsuit Risk At A Glance

- 2,045ADA website accessibility lawsuits filed in U.S. courts from January to June 2026, up 1.54% on a year earlierSource: [EcomBack 2026 mid-year report](https://www.ecomback.com/ada-website-lawsuits-recap-report/2026-mid-year-ada-website-lawsuit-report)

- 24.25%Share of those lawsuits (496) filed against sites that already had an accessibility widget installedSource: [EcomBack 2026 mid-year report](https://www.ecomback.com/ada-website-lawsuits-recap-report/2026-mid-year-ada-website-lawsuit-report)

- $1MPaid by overlay vendor accessiBe under a 2025 FTC order over claims its widget could make any site WCAG compliantSource: [FTC press release, April 2025](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/04/ftc-approves-final-order-requiring-accessibe-pay-1-million)

For most sites, yes, by a wide margin. Defense, settlements, experts and remediation after a demand letter routinely cost far more than a planned audit, and a widget is not a defense. Our fixed packages ($500 Quick, $2,000 Complete, $2,000 [Shopify Accessibility Audit](https://halfaccessible.com/service/shopify-accessibility-audit/)) give you a documented WCAG 2.2 baseline before lawyers or buyers ask. Already received a letter? See [ADA lawsuit remediation](https://halfaccessible.com/ada-lawsuit-remediation/). For market ranges and lawsuit context, see our [accessibility audit cost guide](https://halfaccessible.com/accessibility-audit-cost/) and [ADA website lawsuit statistics 2026](https://halfaccessible.com/ada-website-lawsuit-statistics-2026/).

### Why a Free Scan Is Not the Same as an Audit

We run automated checkers in every audit, but the [W3C Web Accessibility Initiative](https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/tools/selecting/) is clear that evaluation tools “can not determine accessibility, they can only assist in doing so.” That manual work is what you pay for.

An Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) is a document that explains how information and communication technology (ICT) products such as software, hardware, electronic content, and support documentation meet (conform to) the [Revised 508 Standards](https://www.access-board.gov/guidelines-and-standards/communications-and-it/about-the-ict-refresh/final-rule) for IT accessibility. ACRs help Federal agency contracting officials and government buyers to assess ICT for accessibility when doing market research and evaluating proposals.

Government solicitations which include ICT will specify accessibility requirements, indicating which provisions are required to ensure the deliverable is accessible. An ACR is a good way to address the accessibility requirements defined in the solicitation.

We recommend that vendors generate an ACR for any ICT that’s intended to be marketed to the Federal government. Use the ACR to make specific statements in simple recommended language to demonstrate how the features and functional characteristics of your product meet the [Revised 508 Standards](https://www.access-board.gov/guidelines-and-standards/communications-and-it/about-the-ict-refresh/final-rule). Include the [Issue Detail Supplement](https://www.section508.gov/sell/acr-supplement) to provide additional product details, helpful to Federal buyers.

- [ACR Editor](https://acreditor.section508.gov/) - Create portable, machine-readable ACR documents in [OpenACR format](https://github.com/gsa/openacr)

- [How to Create an Accessibility Conformance Report Using A Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT®)](https://www.section508.gov/sell/how-to-create-acr-with-vpat/)

- Make it easy to find your product’s ACR on your company’s website (e.g., link to it on the product description page).

## Related Resources

- [Issue Detail Supplement](https://www.section508.gov/sell/acr-supplement)

## Conduct an audit to measure compliance with laws, guidelines, and standards

 The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is a civil rights and equal opportunity law prohibiting discrimination against people with disabilities in the United States.

 The Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA) is a law established in Ontario, Canada to enforce accessibility standards for government, businesses, nonprofits, private and public sector organizations.

 The European Accessibility Act (EAA) is a directive of the European Union that aims to improve accessibility across all 27 EU member states and for the organizations doing business there.

 EN 301 549 is the European standard of Accessibility requirements for Information and Communications Technology (ICT) products and services in the European Union.

 Section 508 is a sub-section of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 that prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability in federal programs or programs receiving federal aid or employment in the United States.

 The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines were developed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) and are widely accepted as the go-to standard for digital accessibility conformance.

Offering an accessible reading experience can prove to be quite complex. What people want and need can vary significantly, often based not just on accessibility needs from the format (audio, large print, braille, synchronized highlighting), but also ways to engage and interact with the text, especially for educational materials.

Throughout 2025 work was undertaken to identify and document the functionality users want from a current accessible reading solution. This was designed primarily to aid developers working on specialist reading apps, but will also be of use to those working on mainstream reading apps.

This work was grounded in the needs of users, with contributions from individuals, user organizations, content providers, app developers and accessibility experts.

With their help more than 120 user requirements were documented under 11 themes to aid navigation and technical reference. These themes include:

- Screen Reader Support

- Read Aloud

- Embedded Audio

- Visual Adjustments

- Bookmarking

- Highlighting

- Making Notes

- Entering Answers

- Library and Bookshelf

The requirements are supported by 18 unique user stories that highlight how users benefit from the recommended functionality, providing a useful resource in a format commonly used by developers.

Further user requirements were documented for future consideration but not prioritized for the current version of the publication. These include topics like AI assisted features.

Feedback from the wider community has been incredibly positive, with many app developers sharing the user stories with their team and adding recommended features to their development roadmap.

The [Reading Apps User Requirements](https://daisy.org/s/readingURS/) were formally approved and endorsed by the DAISY Board at the meeting in November 2025. Thanks to everyone who contributed to this work.

You can read more about this project in the [Reading Apps User Requirements Project Area.](https://daisy.org/activities/standards/reading-apps-user-requirements/)

The current Reading Apps User Requirements can be referenced using the following short link:

[https://daisy.org/s/readingURS/](https://daisy.org/s/readingURS/)
